alphabet.title: The musical alphabet
alphabet.summary: Seven letters, octaves, and where the natural notes live on your instrument.

blocks.md: Music uses seven letter names: **A B C D E F G**. After G you loop back to A. Each time you come back around to the same letter you've gone up an **octave**. Two notes an octave apart sound like the same note, one higher.
On the piano the black keys come in groups of two and three. **C** is the white key just left of each group of two. From there the white keys run C D E F G A B, then C again.

The six open strings, low to high, are **E A D G B E** (one way to remember: _Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie_). Every fret raises the note by the smallest step. The natural notes aren't evenly spaced along a string, which is why fretboard knowledge takes reps. Fret 12 is the octave, where the pattern starts over.

The four open strings, low to high, are **E A D G**, the same as the lowest four guitar strings but an octave down. Every fret raises the note by the smallest step, and fret 12 is the octave where the pattern repeats.

blocks.name: notes
blocks.caption: Every natural note is labeled. Tap one to hear it and see the same letter everywhere else.

homework: Say the musical alphabet out loud starting on {pick:C|D|E|F|G|A|B}, forward then backward, three times.

homework.piano: Play every {pick:C|F|G|D|A} on the keyboard from lowest to highest, naming each one.
homework.fretted: Find every {pick:C|F|G|D|A} on frets 0 to 12 without looking at the app, then check yourself in the Find the notes drill.

homework.piano: Play C D E F G A B C slowly with your right hand, saying each name.
homework.fretted: Play all the natural notes on the {lowstring} string from fret 0 to 12, saying each name.

homework: Spend two minutes in the Find the notes drill with naturals only.

halfwhole.title: Sharps, flats, half & whole steps
halfwhole.summary: The 12 notes, how sharps and flats work, and the two spots with no note in between.

blocks.md:
Between most natural notes there's one more note. Count them all and you get **12 different notes** before the pattern repeats.

A **half step** is the smallest move: one key to the very next key (black or white) on piano, or one fret on guitar and bass. A **whole step** is two half steps.

A **sharp (♯)** raises a note a half step. A **flat (♭)** lowers it. The note between C and D can be called C♯ or D♭: same sound, two names. Which name you use depends on the key you're in, which the scales unit explains.

Two pairs have nothing in between: **E–F** and **B–C**. They're already a half step apart.
You can see this on the keyboard: there's no black key between E and F, or between B and C.
On the fretboard, E to F and B to C are one fret apart. Every other pair of natural notes is two frets apart.
On the fretboard, E to F and B to C are one fret apart. Every other pair of natural notes is two frets apart.

blocks.name: notes
blocks.caption: All 12 notes. Tap any to hear it and see where else it lives.

homework: Starting on {pick:C|G|D}, play up 12 half steps to the octave, naming each note with a sharp name. Then come back down using flat names.

homework.piano: Play every E–F and B–C pair on the keyboard and notice there is no black key between them.
homework.fretted: On one string, play E to F and B to C (one fret each), then F to G (two frets). Feel the difference.

homework: Pick any note and play a whole step up, then a half step up, then a whole step up. Name each note.

staff.title: Reading notes on the staff
staff.summary: Lines, spaces, clefs, and ledger lines.

blocks.md:
The staff is five lines. Every line and every space is one letter name, moving up the alphabet as you go up. A **clef** tells you which letter goes where.

**Treble clef** (guitar and the piano's right hand): lines from the bottom are **E G B D F** (_Every Good Boy Does Fine_). Spaces spell **F A C E**.

**Bass clef** (bass and the piano's left hand): lines are **G B D F A** (_Good Boys Do Fine Always_). Spaces are **A C E G** (_All Cows Eat Grass_).

Notes above or below the staff get short **ledger lines**. Middle C sits on one ledger line below the treble staff, or one above the bass staff.
Guitar music is written in treble clef but sounds an octave lower than written. The note names don't change.
Bass music is written in bass clef and sounds an octave lower than written. The note names don't change.

blocks.name: staff
blocks.caption: Tap any line or space to hear it and see its name.

homework.piano: Write the treble and bass clef line and space mnemonics from memory on paper.
homework.guitar: Write the treble clef line and space mnemonics from memory on paper.
homework.bass: Write the bass clef line and space mnemonics from memory on paper.

homework: Draw a five-line staff on paper and write the notes C D E F G A B C going up. Check them against the staff explorer.
Do one round of the Staff sprint drill and beat your score.

recipe.title: The major scale recipe
recipe.summary: W W H W W W H, scale degrees, and the one-letter-each spelling rule.

blocks.md:
A scale is a set of notes in order from one note up to its octave. The **major scale** is the one most music is built from, and it follows a fixed pattern of steps:

## W W H W W W H

Think of it as a stencil: slide it to start on any note and it tells you which notes to use. Start on C and you land on only natural notes: C D E F G A B C. The half steps fall between E–F (3 to 4) and B–C (7 to 8).

Number the notes 1 through 7. These **scale degrees** let you talk about music without caring about the key: "the 5" in C is G, "the 5" in D is A.

Spelling rule: a major scale uses **each letter exactly once**. So in G major the 7th note is F♯, never G♭, because G is already taken.

homework: Write W W H W W W H on a sticky note and put it where you practice.
Play C major up and down twice, saying the degree numbers (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8) instead of the letters.
Build {pick:G|F} major on paper using only the recipe, then check it in the explorer.

sharps.title: Major scales with sharps
sharps.summary: G, D, A, E and B major. Each new key adds one sharp.

blocks.md:
Run the recipe from G: G A B C D E **F♯** G. To keep the half step between 7 and 8, F has to go up to F♯.

Now start from D, the 5th note of G major: D E **F♯** G A B **C♯** D. You keep F♯ and pick up C♯. Every time you start a new scale on the 5th of the last one, you add one sharp. That's the circle of fifths showing up early; unit 3 covers it properly.

Keys in this lesson: **G** (1♯), **D** (2♯), **A** (3♯), **E** (4♯), **B** (5♯).
On guitar, one major scale shape is movable: play it from the root on the low E string and slide the whole shape to change keys. Use the explorer below to see each key's notes in place.
On bass, a one-octave major scale fits in one position: root with your 2nd finger, then 4-1-2-4 on the next strings. Slide it anywhere to change keys.

homework: Play {pick:G|D|A|E|B} major up and down two octaves, saying the note names.
Write out all five sharp-key scales (G D A E B) on paper from memory. Check them in the explorer.
Play D major, then A major, and listen for the one note that changes (G becomes G♯).

flats.title: Major scales with flats
flats.summary: F, B♭, E♭, A♭ and D♭ major. Each new key adds one flat.

blocks.md:
Flat keys come from going the other way. Start on F: F G A **B♭** C D E F. The half step between 3 and 4 needs B lowered to B♭.

Each key a 5th lower (the 4th note of the last key) adds a flat: **F** (1♭), **B♭** (2♭), **E♭** (3♭), **A♭** (4♭), **D♭** (5♭).

Same spelling rule: each letter once. In F major the 4th note is B♭, never A♯, because A is already the 3rd.

homework: Play {pick:F|B♭|E♭|A♭|D♭} major up and down two times, naming the notes with flats.
Write F major on paper. Then explain to yourself why its 4th note is B♭ and never A♯.
Pick one sharp key and one flat key. Play them back to back and name every note.

circle.title: Going around the circle
circle.summary: Fifths clockwise, fourths counter-clockwise, and why neighbors matter.

blocks.md:
Put the 12 keys in a ring where each step clockwise goes up a **perfect 5th** (7 half steps). That's the circle of fifths.

Clockwise from C adds one sharp each step: **C G D A E B F♯**. Counter-clockwise adds one flat each step: **C F B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭**. At the bottom, F♯ and G♭ are the same notes on your instrument with different names.

Why it matters: neighbors on the circle share all but one note. That makes them easy to move between, and it's why so many songs borrow chords from the keys right next door. Unit 6 builds on this.

Memory aid for the sharp side: _Good Deeds Always Earn Blessings_.
On guitar, a 5th up is one string higher and two frets up (on the low four strings). You can walk the circle with one shape.
On bass, a 5th up is one string higher and two frets up. A 4th up is straight across to the next string, same fret. You can walk the circle without moving much.

homework: Draw the circle of fifths from memory, outer ring only. Check it against the app.
Play the root notes around the circle clockwise: C G D A E B F♯ D♭ A♭ E♭ B♭ F C.
Say the circle counter-clockwise from C out loud without stopping.

keysig.title: Key signatures
keysig.summary: The order of sharps and flats, and two shortcuts to name any key.

blocks.md:
Instead of writing a sharp on every F in a G major song, music puts the sharps or flats once at the start of each line. That's the **key signature**.

Sharps always appear in the same order: **F C G D A E B** (_Father Charles Goes Down And Ends Battle_). Flats are the same list backwards: **B E A D G C F**.

Two shortcuts:

- **Sharp keys:** the last sharp is the 7th note, so go up a half step to find the key. Last sharp C♯ → D major.
- **Flat keys:** the second-to-last flat is the key. B♭ E♭ A♭ → E♭ major. F major (one flat) you just memorize.

homework: Write the order of sharps and the order of flats on paper five times each.
Name the key signature of {pick:A|E|E♭|A♭|B|D♭} major using only the shortcuts, then check it in the explorer.
Find a piece of sheet music (any song) and name its key from the key signature.

relative.title: Relative minor keys
relative.summary: Same notes, different home. The inner ring of the circle.

blocks.md:
Every major key has a minor key that uses the exact same notes and key signature. That's its **relative minor**.

It starts on the **6th note** of the major scale. C major is C D E F G A B, so the relative minor is **A minor**: same notes, but A is home.

Shortcut: go **down three half steps** from the major key. G → E minor. F → D minor.

On the circle, the relative minor sits on the inner ring right below its major.

homework: Play {pick:C major then A minor|G major then E minor|F major then D minor} scales back to back. Same notes, different home. Listen for the mood change.
Write the inner ring of the circle (all 12 relative minors) from memory.
Think of a song you know in a minor key and figure out its relative major.

intervals.title: Measuring distance: intervals
intervals.summary: Letter count for the number, half steps for the quality.

blocks.md:
An **interval** is the distance between two notes. It has two parts.

**Number:** count letter names, including both ends. C up to E is C-D-E, three letters, so it's a 3rd.

**Quality:** count half steps to tell the versions apart. C to E is 4 half steps, a **major 3rd**. C to E♭ is 3, a **minor 3rd**.

- **minor 2nd**: 1 half step · C → D♭
- **major 2nd**: 2 half steps · C → D
- **minor 3rd**: 3 half steps · C → E♭
- **major 3rd**: 4 half steps · C → E
- **perfect 4th**: 5 half steps · C → F
- **tritone (aug. 4th)**: 6 half steps · C → F♯
- **perfect 5th**: 7 half steps · C → G
- **minor 6th**: 8 half steps · C → A♭
- **major 6th**: 9 half steps · C → A
- **minor 7th**: 10 half steps · C → B♭
- **major 7th**: 11 half steps · C → B
- **octave**: 12 half steps · C → C

From the root of a major scale, the 2nd, 3rd, 6th and 7th are all **major**. The 4th, 5th and octave are called **perfect**.

homework: Learn one song-start per interval: "Here Comes the Bride" starts with a perfect 4th, "Twinkle Twinkle" jumps a perfect 5th. Hum each.
From {pick:C|G|D|A}, play every interval from a minor 2nd up to the octave, naming each.

homework.piano: Play major 3rds and minor 3rds from every white key and listen to the difference.
homework.fretted: Find a major 3rd and a perfect 5th above any note on the {lowstring} string without counting frets one by one.

triads.title: Major and minor triads

blocks.md:
A **triad** is three notes stacked in thirds: a root, a 3rd and a 5th. Take notes 1, 3 and 5 of a major scale and you've got a major triad: C major scale → **C E G**.

The 3rd sets the mood. A **major** triad is a major 3rd (4 half steps) with a minor 3rd (3) on top. A **minor** triad flips it: minor 3rd on the bottom, major 3rd on top. Lower the 3rd of C major (E → E♭) and you get C minor: **C E♭ G**.

Naming: a letter alone means major (G). Add **m** for minor (Gm).
The guitar shapes here are the two movable barre shapes: root on the 6th string (E shape) or the 5th string (A shape).
On bass, chords are usually played one note at a time (an arpeggio). The shape shown is root, 3rd and 5th in one position.

homework: Spell and play the major and minor triads on {pick:C, F and G|G, C and D|A, D and E}.

homework.guitar: Play an E-shape barre chord, then lift one finger to make it minor. Name the note that changed.
homework.bass: Play root-3-5 arpeggios for C, F and G major, then make each one minor.
homework.piano: Play every white-key major triad, then make each one minor by lowering the middle note.

homework: Listen to a song you like and decide if each chord sounds major or minor.

dimaug.title: Diminished and augmented
dimaug.summary: The other two triads: two minor 3rds, or two major 3rds.

blocks.md:
Two more triads finish the set.

**Diminished**: two minor 3rds stacked (3 + 3 half steps). Root, ♭3, ♭5. B D F is **B°**. It sounds tense and unstable.

**Augmented**: two major 3rds (4 + 4). Root, 3, ♯5. C E G♯ is **C+**. It sounds like it hasn't landed anywhere.

- **major**: 1 3 5 · C E G
- **minor**: 1 ♭3 5 · C E♭ G
- **diminished**: 1 ♭3 ♭5 · C E♭ G♭
- **augmented**: 1 3 ♯5 · C E G♯

homework: Play C, Cm, C° and C+ back to back. Name what changes each time.
Spell the diminished triad on B and on F♯ on paper.
Build an augmented triad on C, E and G♯. Notice they contain the same three notes.

sevenths.title: Seventh chords
sevenths.summary: Add one more third: maj7, 7, m7 and m7♭5.

blocks.md:
Add one more third on top of a triad and you get a **seventh chord**: 1, 3, 5, 7.

- **Major 7** (Cmaj7): major triad + major 7th → C E G B. Smooth and jazzy.
- **Dominant 7** (C7): major triad + minor 7th → C E G B♭. Bluesy, and it wants to resolve. This is the V7 chord.
- **Minor 7** (Cm7): minor triad + minor 7th → C E♭ G B♭.
- **Half-diminished** (Cm7♭5): diminished triad + minor 7th → C E♭ G♭ B♭.

homework: Play Gmaj7, G7 and Gm7 back to back and describe how each one feels.
Spell the dominant 7th chord in five keys: C7 F7 G7 D7 A7.
Find a blues recording and listen for the dominant 7th sound.

diatonic.title: Chords in a key
diatonic.summary: Seven chords from one scale: I ii iii IV V vi vii°.

blocks.md:
Build a triad on every note of a major scale, using only notes from that scale, and you get seven chords that belong to the key.

The pattern of qualities is the same in every major key: **Major, minor, minor, Major, Major, minor, diminished**.

Roman numerals label them by degree. Upper case is major, lower case is minor: **I ii iii IV V vi vii°**.

In C: C Dm Em F G Am B°. In G: G Am Bm C D Em F♯°. Numerals let you describe a song once and play it in any key.

homework: Play all seven chords in {pick:G|D|C|A} major, saying the numeral as you play each one.
Write the chords of F major and B♭ major on paper using the M m m M M m dim pattern.
Pick a simple song you know and write its chords as Roman numerals.

progressions.title: Common progressions
progressions.summary: The handful of chord sequences behind a huge share of songs.

blocks.md:
A **progression** is a sequence of chords. A few of them cover a huge share of popular music:

- **I–IV–V–I**: the backbone of rock, folk and country. In G: G C D G.
- **I–V–vi–IV**: the pop "four chords". In C: C G Am F.
- **I–vi–IV–V**: 1950s doo-wop.
- **ii–V–I**: the core move in jazz. In C: Dm G C.
- **12-bar blues**: I I I I · IV IV I I · V IV I V, usually with dominant 7th chords.

V to I is the strongest pull in music. The V chord contains the 7th note of the scale, a half step below home, and your ear wants it to resolve up.

homework: Play I–V–vi–IV in {pick:G|C|D}, four times through, then try it in a second key.
Play a 12-bar blues in {pick:A|E|G} with 7th chords. Count the bars out loud.
Find two songs you know that use I–V–vi–IV.

circleprog.title: The circle as a chord map
circleprog.summary: Six chords of any key sit in one slice of the circle.

blocks.md:
Pick any major key on the circle. The keys on either side are its **IV** (counter-clockwise) and **V** (clockwise). The three minor keys right below them on the inner ring are **ii, vi and iii**.

For C: outer ring F C G = IV I V. Inner ring Dm Am Em = ii vi iii. Six of the seven chords in the key, in one slice.

Moving **counter-clockwise** one step at a time means moving down by 5ths, the most natural-sounding chord motion there is. ii–V–I in C (Dm → G → C) walks counter-clockwise. Many jazz standards chain these moves around the circle.

homework: Pick a key, find its slice on the circle, and play all six chords in it.
Play a chain of dominant 7ths around the circle counter-clockwise: E7 A7 D7 G7 C7. Hear how each one pulls to the next.
Play ii–V–I in three keys next to each other on the circle: C, F and B♭.

minor.title: Minor scales
minor.summary: Natural minor (W H W W H W W) and harmonic minor.

blocks.md:
The **natural minor** scale is the relative minor from unit 3, written from its own root. Its step pattern is **W H W W H W W**.

Compared to the major scale on the same root, it lowers the 3rd, 6th and 7th. A major is A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯. A minor is A B C D E F G.

**Harmonic minor** raises the 7th back up a half step, so the V chord becomes major and pulls home the way it does in a major key: A B C D E F **G♯**.

homework: Play {pick:A|E|D} natural minor, then harmonic minor. Listen to the raised 7th.
Play A major then A minor, and name the three notes that change.
Write natural minor scales on E, B and D on paper.

pentatonic.title: Pentatonic and blues scales
pentatonic.summary: Five-note scales with no half steps, plus the blues note.

blocks.md:
Pentatonic scales use five notes. Drop the 4th and 7th from a major scale and you get **major pentatonic**: C D E G A. With no half steps, almost nothing in it clashes.

**Minor pentatonic** is the same idea from the relative minor: A C D E G (1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7). It's the first scale most guitarists learn for soloing.

Add the ♭5 to minor pentatonic and you get the **blues scale**: A C D E♭ E G.
Look at A minor pentatonic in the explorer with the guitar selected: the notes around fret 5 to 8 form the classic "box" shape.

homework.guitar: Learn the A minor pentatonic box at fret 5 and play it up and down slowly with a metronome.
homework.piano: Play {pick:A|E} minor pentatonic over two octaves.
homework.bass: Play {pick:A|E} minor pentatonic over two octaves.

homework: Improvise for two minutes using only minor pentatonic notes over a blues backing track.
Add the blues note to your pentatonic run and listen for where it sounds best.

modesIntro.title: How modes work
modesIntro.summary: Same notes, different home: seven modes from one major scale.

blocks.md:
Play the C major scale but start and end on D instead of C: D E F G A B C D. Nothing changed except where "home" is, and it sounds completely different. That new scale is a **mode**.

Every major scale gives you seven modes, one starting on each note:

- **Ionian** (start on 1): the major scale itself
- **Dorian** (start on 2)
- **Phrygian** (start on 3)
- **Lydian** (start on 4)
- **Mixolydian** (start on 5)
- **Aeolian** (start on 6): the natural minor scale
- **Locrian** (start on 7)

There are two ways to think about them, and both are useful. The **parent scale** way: D Dorian has the same notes as C major, starting on D. The **color note** way: compare the mode to plain major or minor on the same root, and notice the one or two notes that differ. Lesson by lesson we'll use both.

blocks.name: scale
blocks.caption: Pick a starting note and its matching mode to walk through all seven modes of C major.

homework: Play the white keys (or the C major scale on your instrument) from each of the seven notes, one after another. Hum the starting note and listen for how "home" changes.
Write the seven mode names in order on a sticky note: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian, Locrian.
Pick a major key you know well and name the mode that starts on each of its notes.

dorian.title: Dorian
dorian.summary: Natural minor with a raised 6th: the bright minor.

blocks.md:
**Dorian** is a minor scale with one change: the 6th is a whole step up from where natural minor has it. D natural minor is D E F G A B♭ C. D Dorian is D E F G A **B** C.

That raised 6th takes some of the gloom out of minor. It's all over funk, jazz and rock soloing, and in older folk tunes like "Scarborough Fair".

Parent scale: Dorian starts on the 2nd note of a major scale, so D Dorian uses C major's notes, A Dorian uses G major's, and so on.

When to use it: over a minor 7th chord that's acting as the ii chord (Dm7 in the key of C), or anywhere you want minor that isn't sad.

blocks.name: scale
blocks.caption: Flip between Dorian and natural minor on the same root and listen for the 6th.

homework: Play {pick:D|A|E} natural minor, then {pick:D|A|E} Dorian. Say out loud which note changed.
Improvise for two minutes over a single minor chord using Dorian. Lean on the 6th.
Write the Dorian mode starting on G, then check it here.

mixolydian.title: Mixolydian
mixolydian.summary: Major with a flat 7th: the sound of the dominant chord.

blocks.md:
**Mixolydian** is a major scale with a lowered 7th. G major is G A B C D E F♯. G Mixolydian is G A B C D E **F**.

That flat 7th is exactly the note that turns a major triad into a dominant 7th chord, so Mixolydian is the natural scale to play over a 7 chord. It's the sound of a lot of rock riffs, blues-rock, and Celtic fiddle tunes. The Beatles' "Norwegian Wood" is a well-known example.

Parent scale: Mixolydian starts on the 5th note of a major scale. G Mixolydian uses C major's notes.

blocks.name: scale
blocks.caption: Compare Mixolydian with major on the same root.

homework: Play {pick:G|D|A} major, then {pick:G|D|A} Mixolydian. Notice the 7th.
Strum or hold a {pick:G7|D7|A7} chord and noodle over it with the matching Mixolydian mode.
Write Mixolydian starting on F (careful: it has one flat).

lydianPhrygian.title: Lydian and Phrygian
lydianPhrygian.summary: The dreamy one with a sharp 4, and the dark one with a flat 2.

blocks.md:
**Lydian** is a major scale with a raised 4th. F major is F G A B♭ C D E. F Lydian is F G A **B** C D E. That ♯4 makes it float; it's a favorite in film scores, and the theme from The Simpsons is built on it. Lydian starts on the 4th note of a major scale, so F Lydian uses C major's notes.

**Phrygian** is a natural minor scale with a lowered 2nd. E natural minor is E F♯ G A B C D. E Phrygian is E **F** G A B C D. That half step right above the root gives it a tense, Spanish or flamenco flavor, and it shows up a lot in metal. Phrygian starts on the 3rd note of a major scale, so E Phrygian uses C major's notes.

blocks.name: scale
blocks.caption: Compare Lydian with major, and Phrygian with natural minor.

homework: Play F Lydian slowly and stop on the B each time. Then play F major and stop on the B♭. Hear the difference?
Play E Phrygian over a low E note held (or an open E string). Lean on the F.
Write A Phrygian and D Lydian on paper.

locrianFit.title: Locrian, and choosing a mode
locrianFit.summary: The unstable seventh mode, and which mode goes with which chord.

blocks.md:
**Locrian** starts on the 7th note of a major scale: B C D E F G A in C major. It has a flat 2 and a flat 5, so its home chord is diminished. That makes it hard to rest on, and you'll rarely hear a whole song in Locrian. Its job is to fit over a half-diminished (m7♭5) chord.

Here's the practical version of modes: match the scale to the chord.

- **maj7** chord: Ionian, or Lydian for a brighter color
- **m7** chord: Dorian (as ii), Aeolian (as vi) or Phrygian (as iii)
- **7** chord: Mixolydian
- **m7♭5** chord: Locrian

In the key of C, that means playing C major notes over everything, but thinking of D Dorian over Dm7, G Mixolydian over G7 and so on. Thinking this way helps you land on chord tones.

homework: Write the chord-to-mode list from this lesson from memory.
Over a ii–V–I in C (Dm7 G7 Cmaj7), play D Dorian, G Mixolydian, then C major. Notice they share every note.
Play B Locrian and try to make it sound "finished." Notice why it rarely gets used as home.

triadInversions.title: Triad inversions
triadInversions.summary: Same three notes, different bass note.

blocks.md:
A triad doesn't have to be stacked root-3rd-5th. Move the bottom note up an octave and you get an **inversion**:

- **Root position**: root on the bottom. C E G.
- **1st inversion**: 3rd on the bottom. E G C.
- **2nd inversion**: 5th on the bottom. G C E.

It's still a C major chord each time. What changes is the bass note and the feel: root position sounds solid, 1st inversion lighter, 2nd inversion a little unsettled.

Chord charts show inversions with a slash: **C/E** means "C chord, E in the bass," which is 1st inversion. C/G is 2nd inversion.

To name an inversion you see, stack the notes back into 3rds to find the root, then check which note is on the bottom.

homework.piano: Play C, F and G major in all three inversions with your right hand.
homework.fretted: Find C/E and C/G on your instrument (the bass note matters most).

homework: Write the three inversions of {pick:G|D|F} major on paper.
Look at a chord chart for a song you know and find any slash chords.

seventhInversions.title: Seventh chord inversions
seventhInversions.summary: Four notes, four positions, including the 7th in the bass.

blocks.md:
Seventh chords have four notes, so they have one more inversion:

- Root position: 1 3 5 7
- 1st inversion: 3 5 7 1
- 2nd inversion: 5 7 1 3
- **3rd inversion: 7 1 3 5**

3rd inversion puts the 7th in the bass, which pulls strongly downward. G7/F wants to resolve to C/E, the bass sliding down a half step from F to E. You'll hear that move in hymns, pop ballads and classical music all the time.

homework: Spell G7 in all four positions on paper.

homework.piano: Play G7/F resolving to C/E. Feel the bass step down.
homework.fretted: Play an F bass note under a G7 sound, then move to E under C. Feel the pull.

homework: Find a 3rd-inversion chord in a piece of music you know (look for a slash with the 7th).

voiceLeading.title: Smooth voice leading
voiceLeading.summary: Use inversions so chord changes barely move your hand.

blocks.md:
**Voice leading** is how each note of one chord moves to the next. Good voice leading follows two rules:

1. Keep any note the two chords share right where it is.
2. Move the other notes to the nearest note of the new chord.

Take I–IV–V–I in C. Jumping from root position to root position (C E G → F A C → G B D) moves your whole hand up and down. With inversions it barely moves: **C** (C E G) → **F/C** (C F A) → **G/B** (B D G) → **C** (C E G). The C stays put, and the other notes step.

This is why piano parts and string arrangements sound smooth, and it's why guitarists learn the same chord in several places on the neck.

homework.piano: Play C → F/C → G/B → C with your right hand, eyes closed, until it feels automatic.
homework.fretted: Find a C, F and G chord all within the same four frets and switch between them.

homework: Take I–V–vi–IV in {pick:G|D|C} and find voicings where at least one note stays still at every change.
Write the voicings you found on paper.

slashChords.title: Slash chords and bass lines
slashChords.summary: Using the bass note on purpose to build walking lines.

blocks.md:
A slash chord isn't always an inversion. **C/E** is an inversion because E is in C major. But **D/C** or **G/F** puts a bass note under a chord that doesn't contain it, which creates tension.

The most common use is a **descending bass line** under a progression: C – G/B – Am – Am/G – F. The chords stay simple, but the bass walks down step by step: C B A G F. You've heard this in a hundred songs.

When you read a slash chord: play the chord in your right hand (or upper strings) and the slash note in the bass.

homework: Play C – G/B – Am – Am/G – F and listen to the bass walk down.
Write your own descending line in {pick:G|D|A} using slash chords.
Find a slash chord in a songbook or chart and figure out if it's an inversion or not.

susChords.title: Suspended chords
susChords.summary: sus2 and sus4: chords with no 3rd.

blocks.md:
A **suspended** chord swaps the 3rd for a 2nd or a 4th:

- **sus2**: 1 2 5. Csus2 = C D G.
- **sus4**: 1 4 5. Csus4 = C F G.

With no 3rd, the chord is neither major nor minor. It sounds open and a little unresolved. Classically a sus4 "resolves" by dropping the 4th to the 3rd: Csus4 → C. Pop and rock often just leave it hanging for the open sound.

homework: Play {pick:D|A|G}sus4 → {pick:D|A|G} a few times and listen to it resolve.
Spell sus2 and sus4 on C, G and D on paper.
Replace one chord in a song you know with its sus2 version and see if you like it.

sixAdd9.title: 6 and add9 chords

blocks.md:
Two ways to color a major chord without turning it into a 7th chord:

- **6** chord: add the 6th. C6 = C E G A. Sweet, a little old-fashioned, common in swing and country.
- **add9**: add the 9th (the 2nd, an octave up). Cadd9 = C E G D. Bright and modern, a pop and acoustic guitar staple.

Compare with **maj7** (C E G B), which adds the 7th instead. All three are "fancy C," but each has its own mood.

homework: Play C, C6, Cadd9 and Cmaj7 back to back and describe each in one word.
Spell G6 and Gadd9.
Pick a song you play and swap a major chord for its add9.

extensions.title: 9ths, 11ths and 13ths

blocks.md:
Keep stacking 3rds on top of a 7th chord and you get **extensions**: the 9th, 11th and 13th. They're the 2nd, 4th and 6th, an octave higher.

- **9**: 1 3 5 ♭7 9. C9 = C E G B♭ D.
- **maj9**: 1 3 5 7 9. Cmaj9 = C E G B D.
- **m9**: 1 ♭3 5 ♭7 9. Cm9 = C E♭ G B♭ D.
- **13**: 1 3 5 ♭7 9 13. C13 = C E G B♭ D A. The 11th is usually left out because it clashes with the 3rd.

Nobody plays all six notes of a 13 chord on a guitar. Players drop the 5th first, then often the root (the bass player has it). What matters is the 3rd and 7th, which tell you the chord type, plus the color note on top.

homework: Spell C9, Cmaj9 and Cm9 and circle the note that makes each one different.
Play a 7th chord, then add the 9th on top. Listen to the change.
Find a 9 or 13 chord in a funk or jazz chart and spell it.

dim7Altered.title: Diminished 7th and altered chords

blocks.md:
**Diminished 7th** (°7): four notes, each a minor 3rd apart. B°7 = B D F A♭. Because the gaps are all equal, moving it up a minor 3rd gives you the same four notes. There are really only three different diminished 7th chords. It's great for tense moments and for sliding between chords.

**Altered dominants** add tension to a dominant 7th so it pulls even harder to its resolution:

- **7♭9**: 1 3 5 ♭7 ♭9. G7♭9 = G B D F A♭. Dark and classical-sounding.
- **7♯9**: 1 3 5 ♭7 ♯9. E7♯9 = E G♯ B D F𝄪 (usually written as a G). Gritty; often called the "Hendrix chord."

homework: Play B°7, D°7, F°7 and A♭°7. Notice they're the same four notes.
Play G7 → C, then G7♭9 → C. Which pulls harder?
Spell E7♯9 and A7♭9 on paper.

melodicMinor.title: Melodic minor
melodicMinor.summary: Raise the 6th and 7th: minor that climbs smoothly.

blocks.md:
Harmonic minor raised the 7th, but that left a big gap of three half steps between the 6th and 7th (F to G♯ in A minor). Singers found it awkward.

**Melodic minor** fixes it by raising the 6th too: A B C D E **F♯ G♯** A. It's a major scale with a flat 3.

In classical music, melodic minor goes up with the raised notes and comes down as natural minor. In jazz, people use the raised version both ways, and it's the parent of several useful jazz scales.

blocks.name: scale
blocks.caption: Compare the three minor scales on the same root.

homework: Play A natural, harmonic and melodic minor back to back.
Write melodic minor on {pick:E|D|G}.
Sing or hum melodic minor going up, then natural minor coming down.

minorChords.title: Chords in a minor key
minorChords.summary: i ii° III iv V VI VII, and why V is major.

blocks.md:
Build triads on natural minor and you get: **i ii° III iv v VI VII**. In A minor: Am B° C Dm Em F G.

Notice the v is minor (Em). A minor v doesn't pull home very hard. So minor-key music almost always borrows the raised 7th from harmonic minor to make **V major** (E major in A minor, with G♯). That's the chord that makes a minor song feel like it's landing.

So the working set of chords in A minor is: Am B° C Dm **E** F G.

The relative major shares most of these. A minor and C major have the same chords, just a different home.

homework: Play all seven chords in {pick:A|E|D} minor, using the major V.
Play E major → Am, then Em → Am. Which sounds more final?
Write the chords of E minor and D minor on paper.

minorProgressions.title: Minor progressions
minorProgressions.summary: i–iv–V, the Andalusian cadence, and ii–V–i in minor.

blocks.md:
A few progressions show up again and again in minor keys. We write them with numerals counted from the major scale, so ♭VI means "a major chord on the lowered 6th."

- **i–iv–V**: the minor version of I–IV–V. In A minor: Am Dm E.
- **i–♭VI–♭III–♭VII**: a modern pop staple. Am F C G.
- **i–♭VII–♭VI–V** (the Andalusian cadence): stepping down to a major V. Am G F E. Flamenco, surf rock, and plenty of rock ballads.
- **iiø7–V7–i**: the minor ii–V–i of jazz. Bm7♭5 E7 Am.

homework: Play the Andalusian cadence in {pick:A|E|D} minor four times through.
Play i–♭VI–♭III–♭VII in E minor and name a song it reminds you of.
Write iiø7–V7–i in D minor on paper.

secondaryDominants.title: Secondary dominants
secondaryDominants.summary: Borrow a V7 to point at any chord in the key.

blocks.md:
V7 pulls to I. You can use the same pull to aim at any other chord in the key: play the dominant 7th of that chord first. That's a **secondary dominant**, written **V7/x** ("five of x").

In C major:

- V7/ii = A7 → Dm
- V7/iii = B7 → Em
- V7/IV = C7 → F
- V7/V = D7 → G
- V7/vi = E7 → Am

To find one: go up a perfect 5th from the target chord's root and make it a dominant 7th. You'll spot them because they contain a note outside the key (E7 has a G♯ in the key of C).

homework: In {pick:C|G|D}, play I – V7/vi – vi – IV and listen for the outside note.
Write V7/ii, V7/IV and V7/V in G major.
Find a secondary dominant in a song you know (look for a 7 chord on a root that isn't V).

borrowedChords.title: Borrowed chords
borrowedChords.summary: Pull chords from the parallel minor: iv, ♭VI, ♭VII, ♭III.

blocks.md:
A **borrowed chord** comes from the parallel minor key, the minor key with the same root. In C major you can borrow from C minor. The common ones:

- **iv**: Fm in C. Bittersweet; a favorite of 1960s pop.
- **♭VII**: B♭ in C. Classic rock; I–♭VII–IV–I is everywhere.
- **♭VI**: A♭ in C. Big, cinematic.
- **♭III**: E♭ in C.

I–IV–iv–I (C F Fm C) is one of the most emotional moves in pop. The A in F major drops to A♭ in F minor, then resolves to G in C.

homework: Play C – F – Fm – C slowly and listen for the inner voice dropping.
Play I–♭VII–IV–I in {pick:G|D|A}.
Name the four common borrowed chords in G major.

twoFiveOne.title: The ii–V–I with 7th chords

blocks.md:
You met ii–V–I in unit 6. Jazz plays it with 7th chords: **ii7–V7–Imaj7**. In C: Dm7 G7 Cmaj7.

It works because each chord's root falls a 5th to the next (D → G → C), and the voice leading is beautiful: the 7th of each chord steps down to the 3rd of the next (C in Dm7 → B in G7, F in G7 → E in Cmaj7).

Jazz standards chain ii–Vs through different keys, so if you can spot and play this pattern in every key, you can read a large share of the jazz repertoire.

homework: Play ii7–V7–Imaj7 in C, F and B♭.
Write ii–V–I with 7ths in every flat key up to E♭.
Find three ii–Vs in a jazz standard's chord chart.

turnarounds.title: Turnarounds
turnarounds.summary: I–vi–ii–V and friends: getting back to the top.

blocks.md:
A **turnaround** is a short progression at the end of a section that sends you back to the beginning. The classic one is **I–vi–ii–V**: C Am Dm G.

You can spice it up with secondary dominants, turning vi into VI7 (A7 in C) so it pulls harder to ii: C A7 Dm G7. The "rhythm changes" pattern from Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm" stacks these up: I–vi–ii–V–iii–VI7–ii–V.

A one-chord song can feel like it's going somewhere with a turnaround tacked on the end of each pass.

homework: Play I–vi–ii–V in {pick:C|G|F} four times through.
Swap vi for VI7 and hear the difference.
Listen for a turnaround at the end of a verse in a song you know.

tritoneSubs.title: Tritone substitution
tritoneSubs.summary: Swap a dominant 7th for the one a tritone away.

blocks.md:
Here's a jazz trick: any dominant 7th chord can be replaced by the dominant 7th a **tritone** (six half steps) away. G7 can become **D♭7**.

Why it works: G7 is G B D F, and D♭7 is D♭ F A♭ C♭. The important notes, the 3rd and 7th, are B and F in G7 and F and C♭ (= B) in D♭7. Same two notes, swapped. Those two notes are what create the pull to C.

The result is a ii–♭II7–I: Dm7 D♭7 Cmaj7, with the bass sliding down by half steps.

homework: Play Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7, then Dm7 – D♭7 – Cmaj7. Listen to the bass.
Find the tritone sub for D7, A7 and E7.
Spell G7 and D♭7 and circle the two notes they share.

modulation.title: Modulation and related keys
modulation.summary: Which keys are easy to move to, and why.

blocks.md:
**Modulation** means changing key in the middle of a piece. Some keys are much easier to move to than others.

**Closely related keys** share all but one note with the home key. For any major key they are: the keys one step either way on the circle (IV and V), and the relative minors of all three. For C major: G major, F major, A minor, E minor and D minor.

In major-key classical pieces, moving to the V key is the most common modulation. Pop songs love a different move: the "truck driver" key change, jumping up a half or whole step for the last chorus. That one isn't smooth at all; it's meant to lift.

homework: List the closely related keys of {pick:G|D|F} major.
Play a melody you know, then play it again a whole step higher. Feel the lift.
Listen for a key change in a song's last chorus.

pivotChords.title: Pivot chords
pivotChords.summary: Chords that belong to both keys make the smoothest modulations.

blocks.md:
The smoothest way to change key is through a **pivot chord**: a chord that's in both the old key and the new one.

C major and G major share C, Em, G and Am. To move from C to G, play one of those (say Am), treat it as ii in G, then go to D (V in G) and G. Your ear accepts Am as home-key material, and by the time D arrives you're already in G.

To find pivots: list the chords in both keys and see which appear in both lists.

homework: List the chords shared by {pick:G and D|F and C|D and A} major.
Play C – F – Am – D – G and notice where the key changes.
Write your own modulation from G to D using a pivot chord.

transposing.title: Transposing a song
transposing.summary: Move any song to any key with numerals.

blocks.md:
**Transposing** means moving a whole song to a new key, usually to suit a singer's range or to make it easier to play.

The trick is numerals. Turn the chords into Roman numerals in the old key, then read them back in the new key. C – Am – F – G in C is I – vi – IV – V. In D that's D – Bm – G – A.

Guitarists also cheat with a capo: put it on fret 2 and play C shapes to sound in D. That's transposing too, just done by the instrument.

homework: Transpose a song you know into a key one step higher.
Write I–V–vi–IV in five different keys.

homework.guitar: Play a song with a capo on fret 2 using C shapes. Which key are you in?
homework.piano: Play a simple song in C, then in G.
homework.bass: Play a bass line you know in C, then move it to D.

earIntervals.title: Hearing intervals
earIntervals.summary: Name the distance between two notes by ear.

blocks.md:
Ear training turns theory into something you can hear. Start with intervals.

A lot of people use the start of a familiar song for each interval:

- **Major 2nd**: "Frère Jacques" (the first two notes)
- **Major 3rd**: "When the Saints Go Marching In" (Oh, when)
- **Perfect 4th**: "Here Comes the Bride"
- **Perfect 5th**: "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" (Twinkle, twinkle)
- **Major 6th**: "My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean" (My Bon-)
- **Octave**: "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" (Some-where)

Pick songs that work for you. Use the explorer to hear each interval as many times as you like.

homework: Sing each reference song from this lesson and match it to the interval.
Play the Interval Ears game for five minutes.
Find your own reference song for the minor 3rd.

earChords.title: Hearing chord qualities
earChords.summary: Major, minor, diminished and augmented by ear.

blocks.md:
Each triad quality has its own color, and you can learn to hear it in a second or two:

- **Major**: bright, settled
- **Minor**: darker, sadder
- **Diminished**: tense, squeezed, wants to move
- **Augmented**: floating, unresolved, a bit eerie

Start by telling major from minor. Once that's easy, add the other two. Listen to the explorer side by side before you try the quiz.

homework: Play the Chord Ears game until you can get 10 in a row.
Play random major and minor chords on your instrument with your eyes closed and name them.
Listen to a song and decide if each chord is major or minor.

earScales.title: Hearing scales and modes
earScales.summary: Major, minor and modes by ear.

blocks.md:
Scales have moods too. Major sounds bright, natural minor sad, harmonic minor exotic because of the big gap near the top, and the modes each have their color note.

When you listen, focus on the 3rd first (major or minor?), then the 6th and 7th. That narrows it down quickly.

homework: Play major and natural minor on the same root, eyes closed, and name them.
Have someone play a scale for you and guess which it is.
Hum Dorian and Mixolydian and listen for the 6th and 7th.

earProgressions.title: Hearing progressions
earProgressions.summary: Recognize common chord progressions by ear.

blocks.md:
The progressions from unit 6 cover a huge share of songs. Learning to hear them means you can figure out songs by ear.

Listen to the bass first. I–IV–V–I steps up from 1 to 4 to 5. I–V–vi–IV drops from 5 to 6 and back to 4. vi–IV–I–V starts on a minor chord. ii–V–I starts on a minor chord and resolves in three moves.

All examples here are in C.

homework: Pick a pop song and try to identify its progression by ear.
Play I–V–vi–IV and vi–IV–I–V back to back. They're the same chords starting in different places.
Play the Chord Ears game for five minutes.

octaveShapes.title: Finding any note fast
octaveShapes.summary: Octave shapes so you can find a note anywhere.

blocks.md: To play fluently you need to find any note quickly, in more than one place.
On the piano, octaves are always the same shape: eight white keys apart, or your thumb and pinky stretched. Learn to see each note relative to the groups of black keys.

On guitar, two **octave shapes** do most of the work. From a note on the low E or A string, the octave is two strings up and two frets higher. From the D or G string, it's two strings up and three frets higher (because of the B string tuning). Once you know the notes on the low E and A strings, these shapes give you the rest.
On bass, the octave is two strings up and two frets higher. Learn the notes on the E and A strings and use that shape to find everything else.

blocks.name: notes
blocks.caption: Tap any note to see every place it lives.

homework: Pick a note and find it in every place you can, as fast as you can.
Play the Note Hunt game in survival mode and try to beat your best.

homework.fretted: Learn every natural note on the {lowstring} and A strings.
homework.piano: Play every C on the keyboard, then every F♯.

arpeggios.title: Arpeggios across the instrument
arpeggios.summary: Chord tones everywhere, not just in one shape.

blocks.md:
An **arpeggio** is a chord played one note at a time. Knowing where every chord tone lives lets you outline the harmony anywhere on your instrument, which is the backbone of good soloing and bass lines.

Start with triads, then add the 7th. Say the chord tone (1, 3, 5, 7) as you play each note.

homework: Play a {pick:C|G|A} major arpeggio as high and low as your instrument allows.
Play the Chord Tone Hunt game.
Over a slow I–IV–V, play only chord tones of each chord.

scalePositions.title: Scale positions
scalePositions.summary: One scale, several hand positions, covering the whole instrument.

blocks.md: Playing a scale in one spot is a start. Fluent players can play it anywhere.

On guitar, a major scale breaks into five overlapping **positions** that cover the neck. They're often called the **CAGED** system, because each position surrounds one of the open chord shapes C, A, G, E and D moved up the neck. Learn one position at a time, then the links between them. Use the scale explorer's "One position" view and step through the starting frets.
On bass, each position covers four frets with one finger per fret. Learn the major scale starting on the E string, then on the A string, and you can play it in any key by sliding the shape.
On the piano, the "position" is your fingering. C major uses 1-2-3, thumb under, 1-2-3-4-5 in the right hand. Learn the standard fingering for each key so your hand never runs out of fingers.

homework.guitar: Learn one new position of {pick:G|C|A} major this week.
homework.piano: Practice the fingering for {pick:G|D|F} major, hands separately.
homework.bass: Play {pick:G|C|A} major in two different positions.

homework: Play the Scale Builder game.
Play a scale from the lowest note your instrument has to the highest without stopping.

playingChanges.title: Playing over chord changes
playingChanges.summary: Putting it together: aim for chord tones as the chords move.

blocks.md:
Everything in this course comes together when you play over a progression. The simplest strategy that sounds good: **land on a chord tone when the chord changes**, and use the scale of the key to connect them.

Try it over I–IV–V–I. When the IV arrives, aim for its 3rd. When V arrives, aim for its 3rd. You'll hear the melody follow the harmony.

After that, try the same thing over a ii–V–I and then a minor progression. Use the progression explorer to hear the changes while you play.

homework: Over a slow I–IV–V–I, land on the 3rd of each chord as it changes.
Record yourself improvising over a progression and listen back.
Make up a short melody that uses only chord tones on beat one of each bar.
